'''''Alkanna tinctoria''''', the '''dyer's alkanet'''<ref name=BSBI07>{{BSBI 2007 |access-date=2014-10-17}}</ref> or simply '''alkanet''', is a herbaceous [[flowering plant]] in the [[borage]] family [[Boraginaceae]]. Its roots are used to produce a red [[dye]]. The plant is also known as '''dyers' bugloss''', '''orchanet''', '''Spanish bugloss''', or '''Languedoc bugloss'''. It is native to the [[Mediterranean region]]. 

== Description ==

''Alkanna tinctoria'' has a bright blue flower.<!--description of plant, leaves, ... needed--><ref>{{Cite web |title=Alkanna tinctoria Alkanet, Alkanna PFAF Plant Database |url=https://pfaf.org/user/Plant.aspx?LatinName=Alkanna+tinctoria&utm |access-date=2026-06-17 |website=pfaf.org}}</ref> 

The root is blackish outside, blue-red inside, with a whitish core.<ref name="Ward 1911">{{cite encyclopedia |last=Ward |first=Artemas |title=[[The Grocer's Encyclopedia]] |entry=Alkanet |year=1911 |chapter-url=https://d.lib.msu.edu/fa/24?q=grocer%27s%20encyclopedia |page=20}} (enter search term "Alkanet")</ref> 
It is native to the [[Mediterranean region]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Alkanna tinctoria Alkanet, Alkanna PFAF Plant Database |url=https://pfaf.org/user/Plant.aspx?LatinName=Alkanna+tinctoria |access-date=2026-06-17 |website=pfaf.org}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Anchusae Radix. Alkanna Root. {{!}} Henriette's Herbal Homepage |url=https://www.henriettes-herb.com/eclectic/bpc1911/alkanna.html? |access-date=2026-06-17 |website=www.henriettes-herb.com}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Eccremis ramosa Willd. ex Schult. & Schult.f. |url=http://www.worldfloraonline.org/taxon/wfo-0000766253 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210723144113/http://www.worldfloraonline.org/taxon/wfo-0000766253 |archive-date=2021-07-23 |access-date=2026-06-17 |website=www.worldfloraonline.org |language=en}}</ref>

''A. tinctoria'' has 30 chromosomes and is regarded as a dysploid at the [[tetraploid]] level (4x + 2).<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Ahmad |first1=Muhammad |last2=Leroy |first2=Thibault |last3=Krigas |first3=Nikos |last4=Temsch |first4=Eva M. |last5=Weiss-Schneeweiss |first5=Hanna |last6=Lexer |first6=Christian |last7=Sehr |first7=Eva Maria |last8=Paun |first8=Ovidiu |display-authors=3 |title=Spatial and Ecological Drivers of Genetic Structure in Greek Populations of Alkanna tinctoria (Boraginaceae), a Polyploid Medicinal Herb |journal=Frontiers in Plant Science |date=14 July 2021 |volume=12 |article-number=706574 |doi=10.3389/fpls.2021.706574|pmid=34335669 |pmc=8317432 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2021FrPS...1206574A }}</ref>

== Taxonomy and distribution ==

The subspecies ''Alkanna tinctoria'' ssp. ''tinctoria'' is distributed all around the Mediterranean and the Balkans, and eastwards to Ukraine, but is absent from the Alpine region, Corsica and the Balearic Islands. It is introduced in Germany. The species has a large number of synonyms, starting with Linnaeus's ''Anchusa tinctoria'' in 1762.<ref name=POWO>{{cite web |title=Alkanna tinctoria subsp. tinctoria |url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:77228762-1 |website=Plants of the World Online |access-date=1 July 2026}} in tabs "Distribution", "Synonyms"</ref>

== Dyestuff ==
The root produces a fine red colouring material, which has been used as a dye in the Mediterranean region since antiquity. The dyestuff in its roots is insoluble in water but can be extracted using alcohol or other organic solvents such as oils.<ref name="Ward 1911"/> It is used to colour some cheeses and low-quality [[wine]]s.<ref name="Ward 1911"/>

Powdered and mixed with oil, the alkanet root is used as a [[wood stain]]. When mixed into an oily environment, it imparts a [[crimson]] color to the oil, which when applied to wood moves the wood's color towards dark-red-brown (resembling that of [[rosewood]]), and accentuates the grain of the wood.<ref>"Alkanets" in [http://botanical.com/botanical/mgmh/a/alkan024.html ''A Modern Herbal''], by Mrs. M. Grieve, 1931.</ref> In alkaline environments, alkanet dye is blue; in the presence of acids it gradually changes to crimson.<ref>"Alkanet" in [http://www.henriettesherbal.com/eclectic/usdisp/alkanna.html ''Dispensatory of the United States of America'', 1918], edited by Joseph P. Remington and Horatio C. Wood.</ref>

The colouring agent in ''A. tinctoria'' root has been chemically isolated and named [[alkannin]]. In Australia, alkannin is approved for use as a food colouring; in the European Union, it is called E103 but its approval for use has been withdrawn.<ref name="OFF">{{cite web |title=E103 - Alkannin |url=https://world.openfoodfacts.org/facets/additives/e103-alkannin |website=Open Food Facts |access-date=7 February 2026}}</ref> It has been used as a colorant for products such as [[lipstick]].<ref>[https://books.google.com/books?id=sYYIAAAAQAAJ&dq=alkanet%20oil&pg=PA166 ''The Complete Servant''], by Samuel and Sarah Adams, year 1826.</ref>
<!--
In folk medicine, it has been used to treat [[abscess]]es and [[inflammation]]s.<ref>{{cite book |title=Handbook of medicinal herbs |last=Duke |first=James A. |date=2002 |publisher=[[CRC Press]] |isbn=0-8493-1284-1 |edition=2nd |location=Boca Raton, Florida |oclc=48876592 |pages= }}</ref>{{pn|date=February 2026}}-->

In English in the late medieval era, the name ''[[alkanet]]'' meant ''A. tinctoria''. In the centuries since then, the name has come to be used informally for some other plants related to it.<ref>Alkanet in the [http://quod.lib.umich.edu/cgi/m/mec/med-idx?type=id&id=MED1147&egs=all ''Middle English Dictionary'']</ref>
